To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) light regulates the c-Fos protooncogen in the suprachaismatic nucleus, (2) the phase-dependent mechanism is intrinsic to the SCN tissue, and (3) an in vitro slice will provide a useful tool for dissecting signal transduction elements in the light-regulated c-Fos system.

light stimulates c-Fos protein in the suprashiasmatic nucleus of the hamster, with increased expression after exposure to light during the night or during the subjective dark phase of a constant light schedule.

light regulates c-fos proto-oncogene expression in the supraciasmatic nucleus (the circadian pacemaker of the mammalian brain), that this regulation is dependent on the time of day, and that the phase-dependent activation of this gene persists in an acute slice preparation of the hypothalamus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which the suprachiasmic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus controls circadian rhythmicity in mammals.
the mechanisms that control circadian rhythms, and in particular the circadian clock that is located in the hypothalamic suprachiasmic nucleus (SCN).
the molecular mechanisms that control circadian rhythms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the c-fos gene is a transcriptionally regulated gene that is expressed in a circadian manner in the SCN.
the phase-dependent induction of c-Fos in the SCN is a result of an interaction of the circadian and light signaling pathways, and that this interaction is retained in an in vitro preparation.
the SCN contains a circadian oscillator, and that this oscillator is entrained to light by a photoinduction of c-Fos.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that the phase-dependent gating of c-Fos photo induction in the suprarchiasmatic nucleus (circadian pacemaker in the brain) is intrinsic to SCN cells, and we have demonstrated the utility of a slice preparation for studying the molecular mechanism of circadian photo induction.
we have developed a novel in vitro model system to study the molecular mechanisms of circadian rhythms.

the phase-dependent activation of the immediate-early gene c-Fos is a robust and reproducible feature of light input to the suprachiasmic nucleus (SCN) in vivo, and that it persists in an acute slice preparation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the c-fos promoter is regulated by a light-sensitive mechanism that persists in the suprachiastic nucleus (SCN) after the tissue is excised and placed in culture.
light can regulate the c-fos gene in the supratchiasmatic nucleus (the brain's master clock), but only during the night.
we have demonstrated that the phase-dependent activation of the c-Fos protooncogenes persists in an acute slice preparation.
